newsitem.title: JAPAN: Power sales not enough to cure Japan oil firm woes.
newsitem.headline: Power sales not enough to cure Japan oil firm woes.

text.p: Japanese oil firms, hit hard by market reforms, have moved into the electricity wholesale business, but analysts say it may not be enough to fully restore the health of the ailing industry.

"The fact that oil firms have been chosen as electricity suppliers is a bright piece of news, but the industry as a whole is overwhelmed by depressing factors," said Hisashi Gohno, an analyst at Wako Research Institute, a private body.
Oil refiners were among the companies that won recent tenders to supply electricity to six utilities, which was made possible by a revision to a utility industry law last December.
The deregulation is aimed at encouraging competition within an industry previously monopolised by Japan's 10 major power firms.

"We are enthusiastic about starting to wholesale electricity," said a spokesman for refiner General Sekiyu KK, which was selected by Tokyo Electric Power Co Inc (TEPCO) to provide 547,500 kilowatts (kw) for 15 years starting from 2001.
TEPCO also selected Nippon Petroleum Refining Co Ltd to provide 48,500 kw of power for 15 years starting in 2000.
Industry analysts said oil firms need to diversify to survive now that sales of oil products no longer reap the hefty profits they once did.
"Oil companies could easily dip into the red if they rely on oil product sales alone for income," said Masatomo Azuma, an analyst with Yamaichi Research Institute of Securities and Economics Inc.
"They (oil firms) are not thinking of making masses of money from selling electricity, but it will create a stable source of income," Azuma said.

General Sekiyu KK, 49 percent owned by Exxon Corp of the United States, and Nippon Petroleum Refining Co, a subsidiary of Nippon Oil Co Ltd, have seen their profits battered by slumping domestic retail prices, aggravated by tough competition triggered by the liberalisation of oil product imports last April.
Another refiner, Kyushu Oil Co Ltd, was chosen in a tender by Kyushu Electric Power Co Inc to supply 137,000 kw of power for 15 years starting in 1999.

Nikko Research Centre analyst Takashi Kawai said General Sekiyu should be able to increase annual sales by about 20 billion yen ($176 million), based on a price of seven yen for one kilowatt hour (kWh) of electricity.
But he said profits could not yet be calculated as the cost of the project was unclear.
TEPCO's buying tender set the upper limit on offers at 10.2 yen per kWh.
The refiners need to take more immediate steps, however, to pull themselves out of their troubles, said Wako's Gohno.
"Rather than worrying about future income from electricity, oil firms first need to stabilise their main business of oil products," he said.
While retail prices have slumped, oil firms' costs have risen due to soaring crude prices and a weaker yen. The yen has fallen against the dollar by about 13 percent in the past year.

Japan's 12 leading oil firms expect current profits this business year, ending next March, to fall 32.5 percent to a combined 85 billion yen ($752 million), a recent survey by the Trade Ministry showed. ($1=113 yen)
